overview: Merton (1976) took the crash seriously: on top of the usual diffusion, prices jump at Poisson-random times, with lognormal jump sizes biased downward. Conditioning on how many jumps occurred turns the price into a beautifully simple series — a Poisson-weighted sum of Black–Scholes prices, each with jump-adjusted variance and drift. Set the jump intensity to zero and every term but the first vanishes: the model *is* Black–Scholes plus the honest admission that markets gap.

variables.name: Jump intensity
variables.why_it_matters: Expected jumps per year. Even a small λ transforms short-dated OTM option prices, because a single jump can cross the strike in a way diffusion cannot.

variables.name: Mean log-jump
variables.why_it_matters: The direction of surprise. Negative (as calibrated here) means crashes: the left tail fattens, OTM puts price above Black–Scholes, and the skew appears for structural reasons.

variables.name: Jump dispersion
variables.why_it_matters: How varied the gaps are. It feeds the per-term variance σ²+nσ_J²/T — each additional jump makes the conditional world more volatile.

variables.name: Jump count
variables.why_it_matters: The conditioning trick: given n jumps, the world is Black–Scholes again. The series is just the law of total expectation wearing a Poisson coat.

assumptions: Jump risk is diversifiable and therefore unpriced — Merton's original, debatable assumption that keeps the risk-neutral construction clean.
Jump times are Poisson (memoryless) and jump sizes lognormal, independent of the diffusion.
Between jumps, the standard Black–Scholes world holds.
Constant λ, μ_J, σ_J — no clustering of turbulence.
limitations: No volatility clustering: real crashes raise future volatility; here each jump is an island (Bates fixes this by marrying Merton to Heston).
Jump parameters are hard to estimate — rare events give few data points, so calibration leans on the option smile itself.
The diversifiable-jump-risk assumption is economically shaky for market-wide crashes, which are precisely the jumps that matter.
Hedging is incomplete: no continuous strategy replicates a gap — the model prices what it cannot hedge.
when_to_use: Short-dated smiles (where diffusion-only models are hopeless), earnings and event risk, crash-sensitive payoffs, and as the cleanest demonstration of why smiles exist at all.
when_not_to_use: Long-dated options where vol dynamics dominate jump risk (stochastic vol does better), or if a persistence of turbulence after crashes is essential (needs SVJ-type models).
industry_usage: The jump component inside most production smile models (Bates, SVJ, Kou variants); on its own, a standard tool for event-driven repricing around earnings and announcements.
computational_complexity: A rapidly converging series of closed forms — the sum truncates in a few dozen terms; microseconds.
comparison_note: At the money, Merton and Black–Scholes nearly agree — jumps mostly reshuffle tail mass. The visible gap is in the wings: with downward-biased jumps, OTM puts price *above* Black–Scholes and the model manufactures the skew from an economic mechanism rather than fitting it after the fact.
